desc:
You may replace at most one element nums[i] with its square nums[i] * nums[i]. After that, pick a non-empty contiguous subarray. Return the largest subarray sum you can reach.

Examples: [2, -3, 1] gives 12 (square -3 to get [2, 9, 1]); [-1, -1] gives 1 (square one of them and take that single element).
hints: Squaring never makes an element smaller (x*x ≥ x for integers), so using the operation is never bad. Which element should you square?
That depends on the chosen subarray, so run a DP with a flag: plain[i], best subarray ending at i with no squaring, and sq[i], best subarray ending at i that contains the squared element.
plain[i] = max(plain[i-1], 0) + a[i]. sq[i] = max(sq[i-1] + a[i], max(plain[i-1], 0) + a[i]*a[i]): either the square was placed earlier, or it is placed on a[i] now.
editorial: Kadane with one extra bit of state. plain is the usual best sum of a subarray ending at i. sq is the best sum of a subarray ending at i that includes the single squared element somewhere in it.

At index i the squared element is either already inside the run (sq_prev + a[i]) or it is a[i] itself, in which case the rest of the run is whatever best non-squared run ended at i-1, or nothing (max(plain_prev, 0) + a[i]^2). The answer is the maximum over all plain and sq. Because squaring never lowers a value, allowing 'at most one' is the same as 'exactly one'. O(n) time, O(1) space.
solution:
def maxSubarraySumOneSquare(nums):
    plain = nums[0]
    sq = nums[0] * nums[0]
    best = max(plain, sq)
    for x in nums[1:]:
        new_sq = max(sq + x, max(plain, 0) + x * x)
        plain = max(plain, 0) + x
        sq = new_sq
        best = max(best, plain, sq)
    return best
